fact: System Analysis is the systematic process of studying an existing or proposed system to understand its structure, functions, processes and interactions in order to identify problems, determine requirements, and recommend improvements or solutions
System analysis can also be defined as the process of understanding and specifying in detail what an information system should accomplish

System analysis is all about understanding the business and its goals and strategies, defining requirements for information systems that support those goals and strategies, and supporting the business

The purposes of system analysis are to ensure the system meets user and organisational needs, to reduce the risk of system failure, to provide a clear foundation for system design and development, and to improve efficiency, accuracy and decision-making within the organisation

System Design is the phase of system development that involves translating the requirements identified during system analysis into a detailed blueprint for building the system, defining how the system will be structured, how its components will interact, and how it will operate to meet specified functional and non-functional requirements
Systems Design specifies in detail how the many components of an information system should be physically implemented

A Systems Analyst is a professional who investigates, analyses and evaluates an organisation's information systems and business processes with the objective of designing or improving systems that effectively support organisational goals
The systems analyst acts as a link between business users and technical development teams, ensuring that business needs are accurately translated into technical specifications

The seven roles and responsibilities of a systems analyst are requirements analysis, system evaluation, feasibility studies, system modelling and documentation, the liaison role, solution recommendation, and support during development and implementation
Under feasibility studies the analyst assesses technical, economic, operational, legal and schedule feasibility of proposed systems
Under system modelling and documentation the analyst prepares models such as Data Flow Diagrams, Use Case Diagrams and Entity-Relationship Diagrams
A systems analyst is a business professional who uses analysis and design techniques to solve business problems using information technology; essentially a system analyst is a problem solver

To solve a problem the analyst must FIRST understand the problem and learn everything possible about it, including who is involved, what business processes come into play, and what other systems would be affected by solving the problem
After understanding the problem the analyst must confirm with management that the benefits of solving the problem outweigh the costs

When defining requirements the analyst states what specific objectives must be satisfied, what data needs to be stored and used, what processing must be done to the data, and what outputs must be produced
What needs to be done must be defined first, and how it will be done is not important yet
Many different alternatives must be considered, and the challenge is to select the best, that is the solution with the fewest risks and most benefits
Systems design specifications describe the construction details of all system components, including databases, networks, program modules, operating procedures, user interfaces, and conversion plans

Building a system based on incomplete or misunderstood requirements may lead to over budgeting, late delivery, or delivery of a system that does not fully solve the problems it was intended to address

The analyst's approach to solving problems has eight steps in order: research and understand the problem; verify that the benefits of solving the problem outweigh the costs; define the requirements for solving the problem; develop a set of possible solutions (alternatives); decide which solution is best and make a recommendation; define the details of the chosen solution; implement the solution; monitor to make sure you obtain the desired results
A system is a collection of interrelated components that function together to achieve some outcome
An information system is a collection of interrelated components that collect, process, store and provide as output the information needed to complete business tasks

An information system can also be described as an arrangement of people, data, processes and information technology that interact to collect, process, store and provide as output the information needed to support an organisation
The purpose of an information system is to process input, maintain data, produce reports, handle queries, handle online transactions, and generate other outputs

A subsystem is a system that is part of another system, so subsystems are one way to think of a system's components; for example a sales management system might be a subsystem of a customer relationship management system
The approach of dividing a system into components, decomposing a system into subsystems which can be further decomposed, is called functional decomposition
Viewing a system as a collection of subsystems lets the analyst focus attention on a single area of a business, a group of related areas, or the interfaces among areas

A systems analyst requires a combination of technical, analytical and interpersonal skills, and needs to understand how to build information systems, the business they work for and how it uses each type of system, and people and the way they work
People are the source of requirements information, the labour that builds systems, and the ultimate users of the information system

The six fundamentals a systems analyst should understand are computers and how they work; file, database and storage hardware and software; input and output hardware and software; computer networks and protocols; programming languages, operating systems and utilities; and communication and collaboration technology such as digital telephones, videoconferencing and web-based document management systems
TOOLS are software products used to develop analysis and design specifications and completed system components, while TECHNIQUES are strategies for completing specific system development activities

The four types of tools used in system development are software packages such as Microsoft Access and Adobe Dreamweaver, integrated development environments such as Oracle JDeveloper and Microsoft Visual Studio, computer-aided visual modelling tools such as Rational XDE Modeller, Visible Analyst and Embarcadero Describe, and by extension the specifications they create, store, modify and manage
Examples of techniques include project planning, cost/benefit analysis, interviewing, requirements modelling, architectural design, network configuration, and database design techniques

Business knowledge means understanding business processes, organisational structures and industry practices so systems align with organisational goals, including what business functions organisations perform, how they are structured, how they are managed, and what type of work goes on in them
Specifics the analyst needs to know about a company are what the organisation does, what makes it successful, what its strategies and plans are, and what its traditions and values are

Interpersonal skills are the analyst's MOST IMPORTANT skills, because analysts rely on managers, users, programmers, technical specialists, customers and vendors to take a system from initial idea to final implementation

The analyst is a translator for all project participants, translating business objectives into functional requirements, user needs into system specifications, and technical jargon and details into terms non-technical personnel can easily understand
The analyst must be an effective communicator in many contexts, including conversations, interviews, technical reviews and formal presentations

Communication skills matter because the analyst must interact with users, managers and technical staff to gather requirements, explain system concepts and document specifications clearly, which prevents misunderstandings and ensures requirements accurately reflect user needs
The entire process of building, deploying, using and updating an information system is called the systems development life cycle, or SDLC

The NINE principles of successful systems development are: get the user involved; use a problem-solving approach; establish phases and activities; establish standards for development and documentation; justify systems as capital investments; do not be afraid to cancel or revise scope; divide and conquer; design systems for growth and change; and proper planning and project management
Get the user involved: involving users throughout the process helps ensure requirements are accurate, reduces resistance to change, and increases user acceptance of the final system

Use a problem-solving approach: development should focus on solving real business problems rather than merely applying technology, so developers first understand the problem, evaluate alternatives, then select the option with the greatest benefit and least risk

Establish phases and activities: dividing development into clearly defined phases provides structure and control, making projects easier to manage, monitor and evaluate, and ensuring each step is completed before moving to the next

Establish standards for development and documentation: standards ensure consistency, quality and clarity, and standard methods, tools and documentation formats make systems easier to understand, maintain and enhance over time

Justify systems as capital investments: information systems require significant financial resources and should be evaluated like other capital investments, using cost-benefit analysis to determine whether expected benefits justify the costs and risks

Do not be afraid to cancel or revise scope: if a project becomes too costly, risky, or no longer aligns with organisational goals, revising scope or cancelling entirely can prevent further resource waste
Divide and conquer: breaking a large system into smaller manageable components or subsystems simplifies development and reduces complexity

Design systems for growth and change: systems should be flexible and scalable to accommodate future business expansion, technological advancement and changing requirements, which extends useful life and protects the investment

Proper planning and project management keeps development on schedule, within budget and meeting quality expectations, including realistic timelines, resource allocation, risk management and progress monitoring

A PREDICTIVE approach assumes the development process can be planned and organised in advance and the system developed according to plan, progressing through a fixed sequence of phases with each completed before the next begins; it suits systems that are well understood and well defined

An ADAPTIVE approach is more flexible, assuming the project cannot be planned in full in advance and must be modified as it progresses; it handles changing requirements and uncertainty by developing in short cycles or iterations with continuous user feedback and incremental delivery

In predictive approaches the four activity groups are project planning (planning, organising and scheduling), analysis (understanding the business problem and defining requirements), design (developing program structure and algorithms), and implementation (programming, testing and installing)

Planning, analysis, design and implementation are referred to as PHASES and provide the framework for managing a project; the SUPPORT phase, covering upgrade and maintenance after deployment, is part of the overall SDLC but is not normally considered part of the initial development project
In the adaptive approach activities are repeated in short cycles known as iterations or SPRINTS, each producing a working version of the system or a system component

The adaptive phases are initiation and requirements planning (high-level scope, business problem, objectives, stakeholders and major features, with requirements captured at a high level and prioritised by business value and urgency, often as user stories or feature lists), iterative analysis and design, iterative development or construction, and continuous testing and quality assurance
An example of the adaptive approach is the SPIRAL model

Predictive against adaptive, four rows: requirements defined upfront against requirements evolve over time; linear and structured sequence against iterative and incremental; emphasis on detailed documentation against strong user involvement and collaboration; limited flexibility to accommodate changes against emphasis on working systems over extensive documentation

The chosen approach determines how requirements are gathered, how changes are managed, how risks are controlled and how the system is delivered; selecting the wrong approach can lead to cost overruns, delays, user dissatisfaction and system failure
The SDLC is commonly organised into FIVE major phases: Planning, Analysis, Design, Implementation and Support

The primary objectives of project planning are to identify the scope of the new system, ensure the project is feasible, and develop a schedule, resource plan and budget for the remainder of the project
The five activities in project planning are define the problem (business problem and scope), produce the project schedule, confirm project feasibility, staff the project, and launch the project
Feasibility analysis investigates economic, organisational, technical, resource and schedule feasibility

The primary objective of analysis is to understand and document the business needs and processing requirements of the new system; analysis is essentially a discovery process, and the key words that drive it are DISCOVERY and UNDERSTANDING

The six primary activities of the analysis phase are gather information, define system requirements, prioritise requirements, build a prototype model for discovery of requirements, generate and evaluate alternatives, and review recommendations with management

Information is gathered by observing users as they do their work, interviewing and asking questions of users, reading existing documents about procedures, business rules and job responsibilities, and reviewing existing automated systems
The objective of design is to design the solution system based on the requirements defined and decisions made during analysis

HIGH-LEVEL design consists of developing an architectural structure for the software components, databases, user interface and operating environment, while LOW-LEVEL design entails developing the detailed algorithms and data structures required for software development

The five major design activities are design the application architecture, design and integrate the network, design the user and system interfaces, design and integrate the database, and design and integrate the system controls
The objective of implementation is to produce a reliable, fully functional information system and to ensure all users are trained to use it effectively and efficiently
The five major implementation activities are construct software components, verify and test, convert data, train users and document the system, and install the system

Since the cost of bugs can be immense, testing is one of the most critical steps in implementation, and most organisations spend more time and attention on testing than on writing the programs in the first place
Installation is the process of turning off the old system and turning on the new one

The four conversion approaches are DIRECT CUTOVER, in which the new system immediately replaces the old; PARALLEL conversion, in which both systems run for a month or two until it is clear the new one has no bugs; PHASED conversion, in which small parts of the new system gradually replace small parts of the old; and PILOT conversion, in which a small group of users uses the new system before wider use
One of the most important aspects of conversion is developing a training plan to teach users how to use the new system and help manage the changes it introduces

The objective of support is to keep the system running productively during the years following its initial installation, and the three major support activities are maintain the system, enhance the system, and support the users through a help desk

Maintaining the system covers both fixing errors, known as fixing bugs, and making minor adjustments to processing requirements, while enhancing the system covers major changes driven by government regulations, changes in the business environment, new market opportunities, new competition or new system infrastructure

A help desk is the availability of support staff to assist users with any technical or processing problem associated with an information system; training new users and maintaining current documentation are important elements of this activity
Planning phase deliverables are the project proposal and recommendation, investigation report, analysis of alternatives, cost and benefit analysis, schedule, and recommendation
Analysis phase deliverables are detailed system requirements, revised cost and benefits analysis, and a revised schedule
Design phase deliverables are the logical design, technical design, test plans, revised cost and benefits analysis, and revised schedule
Implementation phase deliverables are system elements, implementation plans, contingency plans, end-user training materials, a maintenance plan, operations plans, and cutover or phase-in
Support phase deliverables are maintenance reports and updated system documentation

Feasibility studies belong particularly to the PLANNING phase and evaluate a project on technical feasibility (availability of technology and skills), economic feasibility (cost-benefit analysis), operational feasibility (user acceptance and organisational impact), legal feasibility (compliance with laws and regulations), and schedule feasibility (ability to finish within the required timeframe)

Feasibility studies reduce risk and prevent wasted resources by identifying constraints early, so management can decide whether to proceed, modify or abandon a project, ensuring only projects with a reasonable chance of success move forward
System development methodology refers to the structured approaches, models and techniques used to plan, analyse, design, implement and maintain information systems
Developing information systems without a clear methodology often leads to cost overruns, missed deadlines, and systems that fail to meet user and business requirements

Systems Development Methodology is the standard process followed by an organisation to conduct all the steps necessary to analyse, design, implement and maintain information systems; it is a framework used to structure, plan and control the development of an information system
The methodologies covered are Waterfall, Rapid Application Development, Prototyping, the Incremental model and Agile
The Waterfall methodology is a traditional, linear approach in which each phase must be completed before the next begins, proceeding sequentially like a natural waterfall
In Waterfall the key deliverables for each phase are presented to the approval committee and project sponsor for approval before the project moves to the next phase
Strict monitoring in Waterfall is ensured through extensive written documentation, formal reviews, and user and information technology management sign-off at the end of each phase
The Waterfall model has two very important variants: Parallel Development and the V-Model

The four advantages of Waterfall are that it is easy to understand and easy to use; it provides structure to inexperienced staff; the sequential approach and strict controls ensure adequate documentation and design reviews, giving quality, reliability and maintainability; and progress is measurable

The six disadvantages of Waterfall are that it is inflexible, slow, costly and cumbersome; forward-only progress gives a false impression of progress; there is little opportunity for the customer to preview the system until it may be too late; problems are often not discovered until system testing; it is difficult to respond to changes; and it produces excessive documentation that is time-consuming to keep updated

Waterfall is used when the project is a transaction-oriented batch system; is large, expensive and complicated; has clear objectives and a solution; has no pressure for immediate implementation; has clear and comprehensive requirements; has requirements stable during the life cycle; and when the project team is not experienced or may change during implementation
The Waterfall model is best suited for projects with stable and well-understood requirements, such as government systems, financial applications, and regulatory or safety-critical systems

The Parallel Model is a variant of Waterfall designed to reduce the long development time of strictly sequential phases; it keeps the structured predictive nature but allows certain activities to be carried out simultaneously

In the Parallel Model the overall system is divided into subprojects or modules AFTER the general analysis and high-level design phases are completed; each subproject then moves through detailed design, implementation and testing at the same time as the others, and once all are complete they are integrated into a single system

V in the V-Shape Model stands for VERIFICATION and VALIDATION; it is a variant of Waterfall that emphasises testing at each development phase, keeping a sequential structure but establishing a direct relationship between each development phase and its corresponding testing phase

In the V-Shape Model development activities proceed DOWN the left side of the V while testing activities move UP the right side, so verification and validation are built in from the beginning rather than deferred to the end

The five advantages of the V-Shaped Model are that it is simple and straightforward; it improves overall quality through early development of test plans; project management can track progress by milestones; deliverables are high quality because of test effectiveness; and verification and validation are done early in development

The four disadvantages of the V-Shaped Model are that it is affected by the rigidity of the waterfall model; it does not easily handle dynamic changes in requirements; it does not suit the dynamic nature of the business environment; and it does not contain risk analysis activities

The V-Shaped Model is used when systems require high reliability, for example hospital patient control applications; when all requirements are known up front; and when the solution and technology to be used are known

RAD, also called iterative development, uses specialised techniques and computer tools to speed up the analysis, design and implementation phases, enabling a portion of the system to be developed quickly and delivered to users for evaluation and feedback

RAD emphasises quick development and delivery through reusable components, visual development tools and intensive user involvement, aiming to deliver a high-quality system at relatively low investment cost, and reduces project risk by breaking the project into smaller segments

RAD tools include Graphical User Interface builders, Computer-Aided Software Engineering tools, Database Management Systems, fourth-generation programming languages, code generators, and object-oriented techniques

The five RAD advantages are that focus moves from documentation to code, described as WYSIWYG; user feedback makes the model very effective; the time-box approach mitigates cost and schedule risk; cost of development is lower because the system matches user expectations; and important additional requirements may be identified and incorporated into subsequent versions

The five RAD disadvantages are that users begin to work with a system that is intentionally incomplete, which is the chief disadvantage of iterative development; more speed and lower cost may lower overall quality; user expectations may increase and requirements expand, leading to scope creep; there is a risk of never achieving closure; and developers and customers must commit to rapid-fire activities in an abbreviated time frame

RAD is used when requirements are reasonably well known, the user will be involved throughout the life cycle, technical risks are low, high performance is not required, and functionality is delivered in increments

The Incremental model develops the system in small manageable portions called increments, each adding new functionality and building on previous releases; it combines linear and iterative methodologies and sits between waterfall and prototyping

In the Incremental model customers outline the required services, which are prioritised and grouped into increments; the first increment is defined in detail and developed, and later increments are integrated with existing ones; further requirements analysis can still be done for later increments, but changes for the CURRENT increment cannot be accepted

The seven advantages of the Incremental model are developing high-risk or major functions first; each release delivers an operational product; lower initial delivery cost; a divide and conquer breakdown of tasks; faster initial product delivery; customers get important functionality early; and reduced risk of changing requirements and overall project failure

The five disadvantages of the Incremental model are difficulty mapping customer requirements to increments of the right size; difficulty identifying common facilities needed by all requirements; the need for good planning and design; the need for early definition of a complete and fully functional system so increments can be defined; and the need for well-defined module interfaces

Prototyping builds prototypes early to enable early feedback and analysis; a quick and dirty version with minimal features is built, then reanalysed, redesigned and reimplemented after user reactions, and the cycle continues until analysts, users and sponsor agree the prototype has enough functionality to be installed
There are two types of prototyping: THROWAWAY prototyping and EVOLUTIONARY prototyping

Evolutionary prototyping builds an initial version and gradually refines and expands it until it becomes the final operational system, evolving through continuous user feedback and iterative enhancements; its objective is to deliver a working system to end users, and development starts with the requirements that are best understood

In evolutionary prototyping the designer builds the database, the user interface and the algorithmic functions, then demonstrates the prototype, and the user evaluates for problems and suggests improvements; this loop continues until the user is satisfied and the prototype becomes the final system

The advantages of evolutionary prototyping are that customers can SEE requirements as they are gathered; a more accurate product is developed; unexpected requirements can be accommodated; developers learn from customers; design and development stay flexible; and interaction with the prototype stimulates awareness of additional needed functionality

The disadvantages of evolutionary prototyping are a tendency to abandon structured program development for code-and-fix; lack of careful methodical analysis before design and implementation decisions; a bad reputation for quick-and-dirty methods; overall maintainability may be overlooked; the customer may want the prototype delivered; and the process may continue forever, which is scope creep

Evolutionary prototyping is used when requirements are unstable or need clarification, as the requirements clarification stage of a waterfall model, to develop user interfaces, for short-lived demonstrations, for new original development, and with the analysis and design portions of object-oriented development

Throwaway prototyping, also called rapid or exploratory prototyping, creates a temporary prototype to help users and analysts understand requirements; prototypes explore design alternatives rather than the actual new system, are built quickly and DISCARDED after requirements are clarified, and the actual system is then developed using a more structured methodology

Throwaway prototyping has a thorough analysis phase to gather requirements first; design prototypes are then developed to understand issues that are not fully understood or carry technical risk, which reduces risk and produces more stable, reliable systems

Throwaway prototyping is used when requirements are unclear or users cannot articulate needs easily; evolutionary prototyping is used when requirements evolve and rapid delivery is required, and it risks weak architecture and difficult documentation

The Agile model is a group of software development methods based on adaptive, iterative and incremental development in which every iteration is a complete software project; modelling and documentation overhead is eliminated while face-to-face communication is preferred

In Agile, development is carried out in short time-boxed cycles known as iterations or sprints; each sprint typically includes requirement analysis, design, coding, testing and review, and at the end of each sprint a working increment is delivered for user evaluation and feedback

Agile activities are creation and prioritisation of user stories or requirements, sprint planning and task assignment, development and testing within each sprint, and sprint review and retrospective for feedback and improvement
Popular agile methods are Crystal Clear, Scrum, Extreme Programming, Lean Software Development, and Kanban
The first challenge for project managers is selecting the methodology, and choosing is not simple because no one methodology is always best
The six methodology selection criteria are clarity of user requirements, familiarity with technology, system complexity, system reliability, short time schedules, and schedule visibility
Clarity of user requirements: when requirements are unclear, system prototyping and throwaway prototyping are more appropriate, because they give users prototypes to interact with early in the SDLC

Familiarity with technology: throwaway prototyping is particularly appropriate where there is a lack of familiarity with the technology, because it explicitly encourages developers to create design prototypes for areas with high risk
System complexity: complex systems require careful and detailed analysis and design, and throwaway prototyping is well suited to that, but system prototyping is NOT

System reliability: the V-model is useful when reliability is important because it emphasises testing, and throwaway prototyping is most appropriate when reliability is a high priority because detailed analysis and design are combined with the ability to test many approaches through design prototypes; examples of critical reliability are medical equipment and missile control systems, against merely important cases such as games and internet video

Short time schedules: projects with short schedules suit RAD methodologies because they are designed to accelerate development, and iterative development and system prototyping are excellent choices because the team can adjust system functionality to meet a specific delivery date
Schedule visibility: RAD methodologies move many critical design decisions earlier in the project so managers can recognise and address risk factors and keep expectations in check

No single methodology suits all projects; traditional methodologies are effective for well-defined stable projects, while adaptive approaches such as Agile and prototyping suit dynamic environments with evolving requirements
Requirements discovery is the process and techniques used by systems analysts to identify and extract system PROBLEMS and solution requirements from the user community, working together with users
A PROBLEM is an undesirable situation that prevents the organisation from fully achieving its mission, vision, goals and objectives

Requirements discovery requires analytical, communication and interpersonal skills; analysts must listen carefully, ask the right questions, resolve conflicting requirements, and validate findings with stakeholders to ensure accuracy and completeness
The process of requirements discovery consists of FOUR activities: problem discovery and analysis, requirements discovery, documenting and analysing requirements, and requirements management
Two types of requirements are identified during discovery: FUNCTIONAL and NON-FUNCTIONAL

Common fact-gathering techniques used during requirements discovery include interviews, questionnaires, workplace user observation, document analysis, facilitated workshops or Joint Application Development sessions, and sometimes prototyping to help users visualise features

System requirements are statements that specify what an information system should do and the conditions under which it must operate; they define expected functions, behaviour and constraints and serve as a formal agreement between stakeholders and the development team

In simple terms, system requirements are what the information system must DO, which are functional requirements, or what it must HAVE, which are non-functional requirements; they are also called business requirements
System requirements are developed during the system ANALYSIS phase and provide the basis for system design, implementation, testing and evaluation

The SIX results of incorrect requirements are: the system may cost more than projected; it may be delivered later than promised; it may not meet users' expectations, causing them not to use it; the costs of maintaining and enhancing it in production may be excessively high; it may be unreliable, prone to errors and downtime; and the reputation of the IT staff is tarnished because any failure is perceived as the team's mistake

FACT-FINDING is the formal process of using research, meetings, interviews, questionnaires, sampling and other techniques to collect information about system problems, requirements and preferences; it is also called information gathering or data collection
Fact-finding brings analysts into contact with sensitive information such as company plans, employee salaries or medical history, and customer credit card or social security information
The analyst's ethical behaviour has two duties: systems analysts must NOT MISUSE that information, and must PROTECT it from people who would misuse it

Breaching fact-finding ethics means the analyst loses respect, credibility and confidence of users and management, impairing the ability to do the job; the organisation and analyst could have legal liability; and the analyst could lose a job

A Requirements Definition Document is a formal document that communicates the requirements of a proposed system to key stakeholders and serves as a CONTRACT for the system's project; it gives a high-level description of system functions and constraints, written in business language

Draft requirements are documented with three tools: USE CASES, which describe how actors interact with the system to achieve goals and focus on what the system does from the user's perspective; DECISION TABLES, which represent complex business rules by listing all conditions and corresponding actions in a table; and REQUIREMENTS TABLES, which organise requirements with an ID, description, type, source, priority and status
The requirements definition document is also referred to as the requirements definition report, requirements statement, requirements specification, or functional specifications

There are SEVEN fact-finding techniques: sampling of existing documentation, forms and databases; research and site visits; observation of the work environment; questionnaires; interviews; prototyping; and joint requirements planning

Sampling of existing documentation reviews the organisation chart, memos and documents describing the problem, standard operating procedures, completed forms, manual and computerised screens and reports, samples of databases, and flowcharts and other system documentation

Sampling existing documents gives insight into current business processes, business rules and information requirements, and helps identify redundancies and inconsistencies in processes and recordkeeping as well as data quality issues

OBSERVATION is a technique in which the analyst either participates in or observes a person performing activities to learn about the system; it uncovers informal procedures, workarounds, bottlenecks and inefficiencies that users may not mention during interviews, and gives first-hand understanding of how work is done

The nine observation guidelines are: determine the who, what, where, when, why and how of the observation; obtain permission from appropriate supervisors or managers; inform those who will be observed of the purpose; keep a low profile; take notes during or immediately following the observation; review observation notes with appropriate individuals; do not interrupt the individuals at work; do not focus heavily on trivial activities; and do not make assumptions
A QUESTIONNAIRE is a special-purpose document that allows the analyst to collect information and opinions from respondents, useful when information is needed from many people quickly and at low cost

A FREE-FORMAT questionnaire offers the respondent greater latitude in the answer, with the answer recorded in the space provided; a FIXED-FORMAT questionnaire requires selecting an answer from predefined responses, and its types include multiple-choice, rating, and ranking questions

An INTERVIEW is a technique whereby analysts collect information from individuals through face-to-face interaction; it can be used to find facts, verify facts, clarify facts, generate enthusiasm, get the end-user involved, identify requirements, and solicit ideas and opinions

An UNSTRUCTURED interview is conducted with only a general goal or subject in mind and with few if any specific questions, the interviewer counting on the interviewee to provide a framework and direct the conversation

A STRUCTURED interview is one in which the interviewer has a specific set of questions to ask; within it an OPEN-ENDED question allows the interviewee to respond in any way that seems appropriate, while a CLOSED-ENDED question restricts answers to specific choices or short direct responses

The interview procedure has five stages: define the objective of the interview, select interviewees, prepare for the interview using an interview guide which is a checklist of specific questions, conduct the interview, and follow up on the interview

Guidelines for communicating during an interview: approach the session with a positive attitude, set the other person at ease, let them know you are listening, ask questions, do not assume anything, take notes, and attend to body language, which is the non-verbal information we communicate, including facial disclosure, eye contact and posture

Following up on the interview means validating the documented responses with the interviewee or relevant stakeholders to ensure correctness and avoid misunderstandings, which enhances the reliability of the gathered information

DISCOVERY PROTOTYPING is the act of building a small-scale, representative or working model of the users' requirements to discover or verify those requirements; it is particularly useful when requirements are unclear or when user interface design is critical to system success

JOINT REQUIREMENTS PLANNING is a process whereby highly structured group meetings are conducted for the purpose of analysing problems and defining requirements; JRP is a SUBSET of the more comprehensive Joint Application Development technique, which encompasses the entire systems development process
JRP participants are the sponsor, the facilitator, users and managers, scribes who take notes, and IT staff

The three steps to plan a JRP session are selecting a location, away from the workplace when possible and requiring several rooms equipped with tables, chairs, whiteboard, overhead projectors and computer equipment; selecting the participants, each released from regular duties; and preparing the agenda, with briefing documentation distributed before each session

Guidelines for a successful JRP session: do not unreasonably deviate from the agenda; stay on schedule; ensure the scribe can take notes; avoid technical jargon; apply conflict resolution skills; allow ample breaks; encourage group consensus; encourage user and management participation without allowing individuals to dominate; and make sure attendees abide by the established ground rules

BRAINSTORMING is a technique for generating ideas by encouraging participants to offer as many ideas as possible in a short period of time, WITHOUT ANY ANALYSIS until all the ideas have been exhausted; one goal of a JRP session is to generate possible solutions to a problem, and brainstorming is the common approach used

Brainstorming guidelines: isolate the appropriate people free from distractions; make sure everyone understands the purpose; appoint one person to record ideas; remind everyone of the rules; within a specified period team members call out ideas as fast as they think of them; only after the group has run out of ideas and all are recorded should they be analysed and evaluated; then refine, combine and improve the ideas generated

The three benefits of JRP are that it actively involves users and management in the project, encouraging them to take ownership; it reduces the amount of time required to develop systems; and when JRP incorporates prototyping as a means for confirming requirements and obtaining design approvals, the benefits of prototyping are realised
A use case represents how a system interacts with its environment by illustrating the activities performed by the users of the system and the system's responses
Use cases are regarded as an EXTERNAL or FUNCTIONAL perspective on a business process, showing how users interact with it rather than its internal procedures or technical details

The importance of use cases: they identify and clarify functional requirements, and a well-developed use case diagram captures most of the system's functional requirements; they are very helpful in understanding exceptions, special cases and error handling that developers easily overlook; and the text-based use case narrative is easy for users to understand while flowing easily into the process model and the data model
USE-CASE MODELLING is the process of modelling a system's functions in terms of business events, who initiates them, and how the system responds to them
Use-case modelling has TWO primary outputs: the use case DIAGRAM and the use case NARRATIVE

A use-case diagram graphically depicts the system as a collection of use cases, actors and their relationships, giving a high-level view of the business events the system must process, showing who will use the system and how users expect to interact with it

A use case documents the interaction required between the user and the system to accomplish the user's task; use cases can also be referred to as system activities, and are represented by an ELLIPSE with the name written inside

Use cases are triggered by external users called ACTORS; actors are ALWAYS OUTSIDE the system boundary and initiate or participate in use cases by sending inputs to the system or receiving outputs from it, and each actor is defined based on what they do in relation to the system

There are four types of actors. PRIMARY BUSINESS ACTOR primarily benefits from the execution of the use case by receiving something of measurable or observable value, such as an employee receiving a salary. PRIMARY SYSTEM ACTOR directly interfaces with the system to initiate or trigger a business event, such as the bursar who dispenses cash. EXTERNAL SERVER ACTOR responds to a request from the use case, such as the Financial Director approving cash dispensing. EXTERNAL RECEIVER ACTOR is not the primary actor but receives something of measurable or observable value from the use case, such as a warehouse receiving a packing order

An ASSOCIATION, also called a communication relationship, represents a direct interaction between an actor and a use case, drawn as a simple line; an association WITH an arrowhead touching the use case indicates the use case was initiated by the actor at the other end, while an association WITHOUT an arrowhead indicates an interaction between the use case and an external server or receiver actor

An EXTENDS relationship extracts complex functionality from a use case into its own use case so users can better follow the process; it is optional or conditional behaviour that extends a base use case under specific conditions, and the ARROW IS DRAWN FROM THE EXTENSION TO THE USE CASE BEING EXTENDED

An INCLUDE or USE relationship is used when one use case ALWAYS requires the behaviour of another as part of its execution; the included use case represents common functionality reused by multiple use cases, which promotes reuse and avoids duplication, for example validating a customer both when placing an order and when making a payment

A DEPENDS ON relationship indicates that one use case relies on another for its execution and cannot be performed until the other has been performed; in a bank, withdrawing cash depends on first depositing cash, and depositing cash depends on opening a bank account; a change in one use case may affect the other, which makes it valuable for managing change impact

GENERALISATION or INHERITANCE is used when two or more actors have the same function or behaviour, extracting the shared behaviour into a new ABSTRACT actor; in the bank example Customer is the abstract actor, and Savings Account Holder and Current Account Holder inherit all Customer use cases such as Withdraw Money and Check Balance while having additional specific use cases of their own; it is denoted with a TRIANGLE arrowhead

The SYSTEM BOUNDARY represents the scope of the system, includes the name of the system inside or on top of the diagram, and is a RECTANGLE used to separate the system's internal use cases from external actors

A use-case NARRATIVE is the textual description of a use case, describing how an actor interacts with a system to achieve a specific goal and explaining the sequence of events step by step, without focusing on technical implementation details

The basic elements of a use case narrative are the use case NAME and unique identifier, the ACTORS, the DESCRIPTION or goal, the PRECONDITIONS, the MAIN FLOW or basic flow, the ALTERNATIVE FLOWS or extensions, and the POSTCONDITIONS

PRECONDITIONS are conditions that must be true before the use case begins, and if they are not met the use case cannot proceed; for example to withdraw money a customer must have a valid ATM card and enter a correct PIN

The MAIN FLOW lists the step-by-step sequence of actions between actor and system, describing the ideal scenario where everything works correctly, usually numbered; ALTERNATIVE FLOWS describe variations, exceptions or error situations that branch off the main flow, such as an invalid PIN or insufficient funds; POSTCONDITIONS describe what must be true after the use case completes, such as the account balance being updated

The four steps to produce a requirements use-case model are: identify business actors; identify business requirements and use cases; construct a use-case model diagram; and document the business requirement use-case narrative

Actors should be named with a NOUN or noun phrase; the five questions to find actors are who or what provides input to the system, who or what receives output from the system, are interfaces required for other systems, are there any events automatically triggered at a predetermined time, and who will maintain information in the system

The five questions to find important use cases are: what are the main tasks of the actor, what information does the actor need from the system, what information does the actor provide to the system, does the system need to inform the actor of changes or events, and does the actor need to inform the system of changes or events

A system can be modelled AS-IS, documenting the current state including processes, data flows, rules, users and technologies without introducing assumptions, or TO-BE, representing the desired future state after improvements describing how the system should operate to better support business goals
A process model is a graphical representation of how a business system should operate, illustrating the processes and activities performed and how data move among them

A process model can document the current system, called the AS-IS system, or the new system being developed, called the TO-BE system; modelling as-is helps identify inefficiencies, delays or redundancies so an improved to-be model can enhance performance, reduce cost and increase productivity

A BUSINESS PROCESS is a collection of activities designed to produce a specific output for a particular customer or market; it emphasises HOW the work is done within an organisation, in contrast to a product, which focuses on WHAT

A PROCESS is a set of related activities or tasks performed in sequence to achieve a specific goal or produce a desired output, involving inputs, actions and outputs; it is a specific ordering of work activities across time and place, with a beginning, an end, and clearly defined inputs and outputs, that is a structure for action
A MODEL is a pictorial representation of reality

PROCESS MODELLING is a technique for organising and documenting a system's processes, inputs, outputs and data stores; it is a formal and graphical way of representing how a business operates, and its main tool is the Data Flow Diagram

The importance of process modelling: it lets designers and users focus on the business aspects of systems; it helps developers understand user requirements, design system functionality and ensure the system meets business needs; it is cheap and easy to modify, especially with CASE tools; its non-technical notation is easily understood by business people; DFDs allow isolation of parts of the system at any chosen level of detail; and process models act as formal documentation of how a system or business operates

A Data Flow Diagram shows business processes and the data that flows between them, depicting the flow of data through a system and the work or processing performed by that system; it shows the source of data input, the processes that act on the data, and the data store, without technical details such as programming
DFDs allow the analyst to determine what the organisation does and how the organisation does it

DFDs are purely logical, not physical models; they contain no implementation details; the DFD is drawn first because it lets designers and users concentrate purely on capturing business aspects; and it is not contaminated by distractions of technical details
There are FOUR DFD elements: external agent or entity, data flow, process, and data store

An EXTERNAL ENTITY is a person, organisation or system outside the system boundary that interacts with the system, and is the source and destination of data; it is depicted as a RECTANGLE, named with a descriptive singular NOUN such as Student, Customer, Client or employee, and it does NOT perform processing

DATA FLOWS are directed arrows, also described as pipes, and data flows in packets through them; one flow arrow represents the movement of multiple data items; names should connote the actual information, such as Order Details or Receipt, and are NOUNS

A PROCESS is depicted by a rectangle with round edges and represents an activity or operation that transforms input data into output data; the data flowing out has more value after processing, and a process is always active; examples are Create Student Record, Calculate Purchase Cost and Register Client
A process name must contain VERBS and must NOT be procedural; the manual's own example contrasts 'Add 1 to the counter', which is procedural, with 'Increment counter', which is a process

Hints to identify a logical process: it performs computations; it makes decisions; it sorts, filters or otherwise summarises data; it organises data into useful information; it triggers other processes; and it uses stored data, that is creates, reads, updates or deletes a record

A DATA STORE is a place where data is stored for later use; the data never changes in the store except that it is used as input to a process and the updated data is returned; naming avoids verbs and physical descriptions of how the data is stored, for example Student Master or Client List; it is frequently implemented as a file or database
A data store is DATA AT REST compared with a data flow, which is DATA IN MOTION; a data store is represented as an open-ended rectangle, that is two parallel lines
The notation described is the GANE-SARSON notation; another popular notation is the DeMarco and Yourdon symbol set

DECOMPOSITION is the iterative act of going from one single system to many component processes, breaking a complex system into smaller, more detailed sub-processes, so the analyst moves from a high-level overview to a detailed understanding; each level of abstraction reveals more or fewer details

The CONTEXT DIAGRAM represents the entire system as one single process and shows the data flows to and from external entities; data stores are usually NOT included unless they are owned by systems or processes other than the one being documented; it shows only external entities and the data flows in and out of the system

The LEVEL 0 DFD breaks the main system into major sub-processes, representing the system's major processes, data flows and data stores at a higher level; it shows all the processes that comprise the overall system and adds data stores; ALL PROCESS MODELS HAVE EXACTLY ONE LEVEL 0 DFD

LEVEL 1 and lower levels further break down each process into more detailed sub-processes, continuing until the process is simple enough to understand; for example Withdraw Money breaks into Validate PIN, Check Balance and Dispense Cash
When decomposing a DFD you must CONSERVE inputs and outputs from processes at the higher level of decomposition; this is called BALANCING, and it ensures consistency across all levels

The manual's worked ATM example builds a Process 0 context diagram with the Customer as the only entity, then a Level 0 showing major processes such as Authenticate User, Withdraw Money, Deposit Money and Check Balance with their data stores and flows, then a Level 1 decomposing Withdraw Money
Data modelling is the analysis of data objects and the relationships between them; it is usually the first step in database design and produces a diagram called an Entity-Relationship Diagram

A DFD answers what does the system DO with data, while an ERD answers what data does the system need to KEEP and how is it connected; the DFD shows the verbs of the system and the ERD shows the nouns, and together they form the full requirements picture before a database can be built

Data modelling is the process of identifying the data objects an organisation needs to keep track of, the properties of each object, and how the objects relate to one another; a data model is INDEPENDENT of any database technology, so the same model could be implemented in Microsoft Access, MySQL or any other system without changing the design

The benefits of data modelling are that it clarifies exactly what data the organisation needs to store, reducing missing or duplicated information; it provides a stable foundation for physical database design since tables, columns and keys derive directly from it; it improves communication between analysts, designers and business users; and it exposes business rules and constraints, such as which relationships are mandatory and which optional, before they are buried inside program code
An ERD is built from FOUR main elements: entities, attributes, identifiers and relationships

An ENTITY is a person, place, object, event or concept about which the organisation keeps data; it is a real-world thing distinguishable from other things and ALWAYS HAS MORE THAN ONE INSTANCE, so a single named person is not an entity but the category they belong to is; it is drawn as a RECTANGLE and named with a SINGULAR noun such as Student rather than Students

An ATTRIBUTE is a piece of information captured about an entity, a property of that entity, drawn as an OVAL connected to its entity; only attributes the organisation needs should be included, since every extra attribute adds a column that must be stored, validated and maintained
A COMPOSITE attribute can be broken down into smaller attributes of its own, for example an Address attribute composed of Street, City and State, shown as smaller ovals branching off the Address oval

The IDENTIFIER is the attribute or combination of attributes that uniquely identifies each instance of an entity; it is also called the PRIMARY KEY; a good identifier should never be blank and should never need to change once assigned, which is why systems prefer an assigned ID number over a phone number or email address

A RELATIONSHIP is an association between two or more entities, drawn as a line connecting them and usually named with an ACTIVE VERB such as Registers, Teaches or Supervises, so the diagram reads like a sentence: Student Registers for Course

A relationship line carries THREE properties forming the relationship statement: the LINK PHRASE, which is the verb describing the relationship; the DEGREE or CARDINALITY, which states how many instances of one entity relate to instances of the other; and the PARTICIPATION or ORDINALITY, which states whether the relationship is mandatory or optional
CARDINALITY specifies how many instances of one entity can relate to a single instance of another; there are three common cardinal relationships: one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many
ONE-TO-ONE (1:1) means each instance of A relates to exactly one instance of B and vice versa, for example each employee has one login account and each login account belongs to one employee

ONE-TO-MANY (1:M) means one instance of A relates to many instances of B but each B relates back to only one A, for example one customer can place many orders but each order belongs to one customer only

MANY-TO-MANY (M:N) means instances of A can relate to many instances of B and vice versa, for example a student can register for many courses and a course can have many students; a many-to-many relationship is normally resolved by introducing an ASSOCIATIVE ENTITY, such as Enrolment or Registration, when the ERD is converted into database tables

ORDINALITY states whether the minimum number of instances required is zero, meaning optional, or one, meaning mandatory; for example a Student may be required to have at least one Enrolment (mandatory) while a Course might exist in the catalogue before any student has registered (optional)

An ERD is read one relationship line at a time, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS; in the Course Section, Enrolment and Student example, one Course Section has many Enrolments each with its own grade and each Enrolment applies to one Student, while read the other way one Student has many Enrolments each with its own grade and each applies to one Course Section

The FIVE steps to construct an ER diagram are: identify the entities; identify the attributes of each entity and mark the identifier; identify the relationship between the entities and name it with a verb; determine the cardinality of the relationship; and draw the diagram, placing entities as rectangles, connecting them through a relationship DIAMOND labelled with the verb, marking the cardinality on either side of the diamond, and attaching attribute ovals to their entities

In the worked university example the entities are Student and Course, Student has student_id as identifier plus name, Course has course_code as identifier plus title, the relationship is Registers for, and the cardinality is many-to-many because one student registers for many courses and one course has many students

The earlier modules used STRUCTURED techniques, DFDs to model processes and ER diagrams to model data, as two separate views of the same system; OBJECT-ORIENTED DESIGN instead combines process and data into a single unit called an object

Object-oriented analysis and design is the process of modelling a software application using object-oriented techniques; the system is modelled as a collection of objects that each manage their own data, called state, and their own behaviour, called operations, and a running system is a set of objects sending MESSAGES to one another
An OBJECT is a single instance of something in the system, such as a particular student or a particular order

Every object has THREE things: STATE, the data held by the object represented as attributes; BEHAVIOUR, the operations it can perform represented as methods or functions; and IDENTITY, something distinguishing it from every other object even if its attributes are identical, as two students could share a name but never a student ID

A CLASS is the BLUEPRINT from which objects are created; it defines the attributes and operations all objects of that type will have but holds no actual data itself, only describing the shape every object of that type will follow
Objects interact with one another by sending MESSAGES, essentially calling one another's operations, which is how a system built this way gets work done

ENCAPSULATION is bundling an object's data and the operations that act on that data together and hiding the internal details from the outside, so other parts of the system interact with the object only through its defined operations

INHERITANCE allows one class to be defined as a specialised version of another, for example a Postgraduate Student class inheriting the attributes and operations of a general Student class while adding its own such as a supervisor, which avoids repeating shared attributes and operations

POLYMORPHISM allows different classes to respond to the same operation call in ways appropriate to each class, for example calculateFee() working differently for an Undergraduate Student than a Postgraduate Student although both are called the same way, so the rest of the system need not know which type it is dealing with

The SIX activities of the object-oriented design process are: identify the candidate classes, usually by examining the requirements model built during analysis including the use cases; identify the relationships between classes such as association, aggregation, composition and inheritance; identify the attributes and operations belonging to each class; model the classes and their relationships in a class diagram; model how objects interact to fulfil each use case, typically using a sequence diagram; and check that the classes identified are consistent with the use cases produced during requirements modelling

These activities are ITERATIVE rather than strictly linear: as class and sequence diagrams are built, gaps or errors in the requirements are often discovered and fed back into earlier steps, for example a sequence diagram revealing that a class needs an operation nobody listed

The Unified Modelling Language is the industry-standard NOTATION for documenting object-oriented analysis and design; UML is NOT a method in itself, it is a common visual language that different object-oriented methods can use

UML diagrams are grouped into two categories: STRUCTURAL diagrams describing the static structure, that is the classes, objects and physical components and how they relate, with examples being class diagrams, component diagrams and deployment diagrams

BEHAVIOURAL diagrams describe how the system behaves over time, how objects interact, how control flows and how objects change state; examples are use case diagrams, sequence diagrams, activity diagrams, state chart diagrams and collaboration diagrams
A CLASS DIAGRAM depicts the object structure of a system, showing the classes, their attributes and operations, and the relationships between them
A class is drawn as a rectangle divided into THREE COMPARTMENTS: the class NAME at the top, its ATTRIBUTES in the middle, and its OPERATIONS at the bottom

ASSOCIATION is a general relationship between two classes showing that objects of one are connected to objects of another; it is drawn as a line often labelled with the MULTIPLICITY, such as 1 or M, for example one Student associated with many Enrolment records

AGGREGATION is a special form of association representing a WHOLE-PART relationship where the part CAN exist independently of the whole; for example a Department has Lecturers, but a lecturer can transfer to another department and continue to exist

COMPOSITION is a STRONGER form of aggregation where the part CANNOT exist without the whole; for example an Order is made up of Order Lines, and if the order is deleted its order lines are deleted with it

INHERITANCE or generalisation is a relationship where a SUBCLASS is a specialised version of a SUPERCLASS and inherits its attributes and operations; it is drawn as a line with a HOLLOW TRIANGLE pointing to the superclass
The four class relationships look similar because a line is a line; the small SYMBOL at one end of the line is what tells them apart

The FIVE steps to build a class diagram are: identify the candidate classes from the requirements model, particularly the use case diagram and narratives; identify the relationships and multiplicity between classes; identify the attributes of each class; identify the operations of each class; and check that the classes are consistent with the use cases already produced

In the worked class diagram, Student and Course are the two main classes and ENROLMENT is the ASSOCIATIVE CLASS needed because a student can register for many courses and a course can have many students
Although use case diagrams were introduced as part of requirements modelling, they are also considered a UML BEHAVIOURAL diagram, since they depict how external agents interact with the system
INCLUDE means a base use case ALWAYS requires the behaviour of another use case to complete, for example Record Grades includes Save Grades since every act of recording must end with saving
EXTEND means a use case OPTIONALLY adds extra behaviour to a base use case under certain conditions, for example Place Order extended by Apply Discount but only when a discount code is entered
Include and extend are easy to confuse because BOTH are drawn as DASHED ARROWS; the direction of the arrow and the everyday meaning of ALWAYS against SOMETIMES is what distinguishes them

The FOUR steps to build a use case diagram are: identify the actors, the people or external systems that will use the system; identify the use cases, the tasks each actor needs to perform; draw an association line from each actor to every use case they are involved in; and identify any include or extend relationships between use cases, drawn as dashed arrows labelled accordingly

In the school grading worked example the actors are Teacher, Administrator and Student; the use cases are Record Grades, Update Grades, Distribute Report Cards, Generate Report Cards and View Grades; Record Grades and Update Grades both include a Save/Load Grades use case, and View Grades includes a Login use case

A SEQUENCE DIAGRAM describes the flow of messages, events and actions between objects OVER TIME, showing how objects interact in a particular scenario of a use case, and is used to document the logical ORDER in which messages are exchanged
In a sequence diagram each object is shown at the top of a vertical dashed line called a LIFELINE; messages are horizontal arrows between lifelines ordered TOP TO BOTTOM to show sequence
In a sequence diagram a SOLID arrow represents a call or request while a DASHED arrow represents a return or response, so the arrow style tells you whether something is being asked for or handed back

The FOUR steps to build a sequence diagram are: identify the objects involved and place each at the top of its own lifeline; list the messages that must be exchanged in order; draw each message as a horizontal arrow at the appropriate height, solid for a request and dashed for a response; and number the messages if the sequence needs to be explicit
The worked sequence diagram is an ATM cash withdrawal with three objects, Customer, ATM System and Bank Server, with messages running from inserting a card through to debiting the account

A STATE CHART DIAGRAM, also called a state machine diagram, shows the different STATES an object can be in during its lifetime and the EVENTS that cause it to move from one state to another; it suits objects whose behaviour depends heavily on their current state

In a state chart each state is drawn as a ROUNDED RECTANGLE, transitions are arrows labelled with the event that triggers the change, and the diagram starts from a SOLID BLACK CIRCLE marking the initial state

The worked state chart shows an Order object beginning at Placed, moving to Confirmed once payment succeeds, then Shipped, then Delivered, and able to move to Cancelled if the customer cancels or payment fails, showing not every object follows a straight-line path

An ACTIVITY DIAGRAM shows the flow of CONTROL, and optionally data, through the steps in a process; it is similar in spirit to a FLOWCHART and is useful for workflows, business processes, and the logic within a single use case or operation

An activity diagram is made of ACTIVITY NODES representing the execution of a step, connected by control flows and data flows; it can show DECISION POINTS drawn as DIAMONDS where the flow branches on a condition, and PARALLEL PATHS where two or more activities happen at the same time
A COMPONENT DIAGRAM depicts the PHYSICAL ARCHITECTURE OF THE SOFTWARE: the software components making up the system and the relationships, usually dependencies, between them

A COMPONENT is a replaceable, self-contained part of the system that provides a defined set of services through one or more INTERFACES, and can be replaced with an alternative implementation as long as it honours the same interface

A DEPLOYMENT DIAGRAM describes the physical deployment architecture of the HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE, showing processors, devices and software components and how they are connected, indicating WHERE each part of the system runs; it is the more detailed implementation-level view of the architecture

The worked deployment diagram shows a client device running a browser or mobile app connected over HTTPS to an application server running the business logic, connected over SQL to a database server hosting the DBMS

A COLLABORATION DIAGRAM, also called a communication diagram, shows the SAME INFORMATION as a sequence diagram, objects and the messages between them, but organises it SPATIALLY around the objects rather than chronologically down the page, with messages NUMBERED to show order
Collaboration diagrams are useful when the focus is on how objects are STRUCTURALLY CONNECTED, while sequence diagrams are more useful when the focus is on the exact TIMING AND ORDER of messages
